Based on the healthcare Q&A matches provided, it appears that communication disorders can indeed extend to musical messages. Music is not only a form of emotional expression but also a complex auditory stimulus that can convey various meanings and emotions. People with different types of communication disorders may have varying levels of proficiency in understanding or producing music, as well as differential abilities in processing and interpreting musical signals.

While individuals with certain communication disorders, such as those related to language processing or social interaction, might find it more challenging to comprehend music, others who have conditions like apraxia of speech or dysarthria may be able to recognize and respond to musical messages. Additionally, some individuals with non-verbal communication disorders, such as those with autism spectrum disorder, may still be able to understand the emotional content of music.

It is essential to consider the individual's unique experiences, abilities, and limitations when selecting music for clinical interventions focusing on emotions or movement. Clinicians should take into account these differential abilities when using music in therapy sessions.

In summary, communication disorders can indeed affect one's ability to understand and appreciate musical messages, but it's not a universal aspect of these conditions. A thorough understanding of the individual's needs and capabilities is crucial when selecting music for therapeutic purposes.
